title: Does Lymphoma Show Up in Blood Work? What a CBC Can and Cannot Show
summary: Does lymphoma show up in blood work? What a CBC, LDH and ESR can hint at, why blood work is often normal in lymphoma, how it is diagnosed, and when a swollen node needs a visit.
body_markdown:
Table of contents


Lymphoma usually does not show up on routine blood work, and blood tests cannot diagnose or rule it out. The American Cancer Society states plainly that blood tests are not used to diagnose lymphoma \[[1](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. Many people with lymphoma, even aggressive lymphoma, have a normal complete blood count (CBC) \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \]. Some results can prompt a closer look, such as anemia, a low or high[white blood cell count](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/white-blood-cell-count) , a high LDH or a high ESR. Each of those has far more common causes than lymphoma. Lymphoma is diagnosed with a biopsy, usually of an enlarged lymph node, and a swollen node or symptoms that do not go away matter more than any single blood number.


This page covers one question: what blood work can and cannot tell you about lymphoma, and what to do if you are worried. For leukemia, a different blood cancer that often does change the blood count, see[early signs of leukemia in adults](https://mitohealth.com/blog/early-signs-and-symptoms-of-leukemia-in-adults) .


## The short answer


- **No blood test diagnoses lymphoma.** A biopsy is the only way to confirm it \[[1](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \].
- **Normal blood work does not rule it out.** A 2023 review of lymphoma workup in general practice says there is no single test to diagnose or definitively rule out lymphoma, and that normal results on the usual blood tests should not be used to rule it out \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].
- **Abnormal results are clues, not answers.** Anemia, low platelets, low or high white cells, high LDH and a high ESR can all occur in lymphoma, and all are much more often caused by something else \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \].
- **The body usually gives the first signal.** Most people with non-Hodgkin lymphoma see a doctor because of a lump that has not gone away, other symptoms, or simply feeling unwell, not because of a blood test \[[1](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \].


## What a CBC can show in lymphoma, and why it is often normal


Lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. It usually grows in lymph nodes and other lymph tissue, such as the spleen, rather than in the bloodstream. Apart from forms of lymphoma that spill into the blood, it is rare to see lymphoma cells circulating \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \]. That is the main reason a CBC can look completely normal while lymphoma is present.


A[CBC](https://mitohealth.com/guide/cbc-blood-test-results-explained) counts red cells, white cells and platelets, and measures hemoglobin. The version with a differential also counts each type of white cell, including[lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/lymphocytes) and[eosinophils](https://mitohealth.com/biomarkers/eosinophils) \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-differential/) \]. When lymphoma does change the CBC, the review describes these patterns \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \]:


- **Anemia, low platelets or low white cells.** These can mean lymphoma has reached the bone marrow, where blood cells are made. They can also come from chronic inflammation, iron or B12 deficiency, the immune system destroying red cells, or an enlarged spleen trapping cells.
- **A high lymphocyte count.** This fits some lymphomas that circulate in the blood, such as small lymphocytic lymphoma.


The same review estimates that anemia is present in 32% to 45% of people with untreated lymphoma. Put the other way, more than half of people with untreated lymphoma do not have anemia \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].


## Blood results that can prompt a closer look


Each result below can appear in lymphoma. Each one is far more often explained by something common. What turns a result into a reason for a closer look is that it persists on repeat testing, has no other explanation, or comes with the symptoms described further down.


Result How it can relate to lymphoma Far more common causes


[High lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-lymphocytes) Some lymphomas circulate in the blood, such as small lymphocytic lymphoma \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \]. The National Cancer Institute notes that mantle cell lymphoma can spread to the blood \[[5](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lymphoma/patient/adult-nhl-treatment-pdq) \] Viral infections such as mononucleosis, smoking, stress and some medicines. See[causes of high lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/blog/high-lymphocytes-causes)


High total white cell count The American Cancer Society lists a high white count as one possible sign of Hodgkin lymphoma \[[6](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \] Infection, inflammation, allergic reactions and some steroids \[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-differential/) \]. See[which WBC levels are dangerous](https://mitohealth.com/guide/dangerous-wbc-thresholds)


Low white cells, including[low lymphocytes](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-low-lymphocytes) Lymphoma in the bone marrow can lower blood cell production \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \] Medicines such as some antibiotics, HIV, autoimmune disorders and other bone marrow problems \[[3](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/complete-blood-count-cbc/) \]\[[4](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/blood-differential/) \]


[High eosinophils](https://mitohealth.com/symptom-levels/symptoms-of-high-eosinophils) MedlinePlus lists lymphoma among the causes of a high eosinophil count \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003649.htm) \] Allergies, hay fever, asthma, eczema, parasite infections and autoimmune disease \[[7](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003649.htm) \]


Low hemoglobin (anemia) or low platelets Marrow involvement, chronic inflammation or immune destruction of cells \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \] Iron deficiency is the most common cause of anemia. See[is low hemoglobin a sign of cancer?](https://mitohealth.com/blog/is-low-hemoglobin-a-sign-of-cancer)


High LDH LDH is often raised in lymphoma, especially aggressive types, but it is not specific \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \]\[[5](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lymphoma/patient/adult-nhl-treatment-pdq) \] Any tissue damage, including liver, muscle, kidney or heart injury, intense exercise, some medicines, and red cells breaking open in the sample tube \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/lactate-dehydrogenase-ldh-test/) \]


High ESR ESR measures inflammation and can be raised in some people with Hodgkin lymphoma \[[6](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \] Infections, arthritis, autoimmune disease, kidney disease, pregnancy, aging and obesity \[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/erythrocyte-sedimentation-rate-esr/) \]


High calcium or abnormal kidney or liver tests Fewer than 15% of people with lymphoma have high calcium. Enlarged nodes can press on the kidneys or liver \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \] Parathyroid problems, dehydration, medicines and common kidney and liver conditions. See[is high calcium a sign of cancer?](https://mitohealth.com/blog/is-high-calcium-a-sign-of-cancer)


Two markers are often mentioned online and need context:


- **LDH and ESR cannot point to a cause on their own.** MedlinePlus says an LDH test alone cannot show what is damaging tissue or where, and an ESR alone cannot diagnose which condition is causing inflammation. You can also have an inflammatory condition with a normal ESR \[[8](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/lactate-dehydrogenase-ldh-test/) \]\[[9](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/erythrocyte-sedimentation-rate-esr/) \].
- **Beta-2 microglobulin is not a screening test.** MedlinePlus says it cannot be used to screen for or diagnose cancer. It is used after a diagnosis of certain lymphomas,[myeloma](https://mitohealth.com/blog/multiple-myeloma-blood-test) or chronic lymphocytic leukemia to judge how much disease there is and how treatment is working \[[10](https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/beta-2-microglobulin-b2m-tumor-marker-test/) \]. The[beta-2 microglobulin test](https://mitohealth.com/products/beta-2-microglobulin-serum) is useful in that setting, not as a check for whether you have lymphoma.


## Can you have lymphoma with normal blood work?


Yes. Normal blood work is common in lymphoma and does not rule it out. The 2023 review of lymphoma workup in general practice states that many patients with lymphoma, even aggressive lymphoma, have a normal CBC, and that this should not be considered evidence against the diagnosis. It adds that the absence of abnormalities on any of the usual blood tests, including the CBC, metabolic panel and LDH, should not be used to definitively rule lymphoma out \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].


The reverse also holds. Normal blood work does not prove you have lymphoma either, and most people with a swollen node do not. In primary care, only about 1.1% of people with unexplained swollen lymph nodes turn out to have any cancer. That figure is about 4% in people 40 and older and 0.4% in people under 40 \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2016/1201/p896.html) \].


So the practical answer is to let the node and your symptoms, not the blood count, decide what happens next. A node that keeps growing, does not shrink after several weeks, or comes with night sweats, fever or weight loss needs a visit even if every blood result is in range.


## What actually diagnoses lymphoma


A biopsy diagnoses lymphoma. Blood tests, imaging and the physical exam decide whether a biopsy is needed and help plan care afterward.


- **Lymph node biopsy.** Part or all of an enlarged node is removed and examined by a pathologist. The American Cancer Society calls an excisional or incisional biopsy the most common type when lymphoma is suspected, because it almost always gives enough tissue to name the exact type \[[1](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. Removing the whole node remains the gold standard \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].
- **Needle biopsy.** A core needle biopsy takes a thin cylinder of tissue and can be enough in some cases. A fine needle aspiration, which draws out loose cells, is not recommended on its own to diagnose or rule out lymphoma, because it often misses it and cannot show the node’s structure \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \]\[[12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33175094/) \].
- **Flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry.** These lab tests use antibodies to identify proteins on cells from the biopsy. They help show whether a node is swollen from lymphoma, another cancer or a non-cancerous cause, and which type of lymphoma it is \[[1](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]. Flow cytometry on a blood sample is a different matter. It rarely finds lymphoma that lives mainly in the nodes, and it can miss lymphomas with few cancer cells, such as Hodgkin lymphoma \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \]\[[13](https://www.hematology.org/education/trainees/fellows/hematopoiesis/2022/workup-of-possible-lymphoma) \].
- **Imaging.** CT and PET/CT scans show which nodes and organs are enlarged and guide where to biopsy. They do not confirm lymphoma on their own, and not every lymphoma lights up on a PET scan \[[1](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]\[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].


A biopsy is not always done right away. Because infections cause enlarged nodes far more often than lymphoma, doctors often wait a few weeks, sometimes with antibiotics, to see whether a node shrinks. A biopsy may be done right away when the node’s size, feel or location, or other symptoms, strongly suggest lymphoma \[[1](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \].


## Symptoms that matter more than the blood count


The National Cancer Institute lists these signs of non-Hodgkin lymphoma: swollen lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, groin or stomach, fever for no known reason, drenching night sweats, feeling very tired, weight loss for no known reason, skin rash or itchy skin, and pain in the chest, abdomen or bones for no known reason \[[5](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lymphoma/patient/adult-nhl-treatment-pdq) \]. For Hodgkin lymphoma, it lists painless swollen nodes, fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss over the past 6 months, and itchy skin, especially after bathing or drinking alcohol \[[14](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lymphoma/patient/adult-hodgkin-treatment-pdq) \].


Fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss together are called B symptoms. The American Cancer Society defines the weight loss as at least 10% of body weight over 6 months without trying \[[15](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \]. These symptoms are common in infections too. For other causes of sweating at night, see[night sweats in women](https://mitohealth.com/symptoms/night-sweats-in-women) .


### Symptom and result patterns worth a visit


These combinations come from published referral and workup guidance. None of them means you have lymphoma. Each is a reason to have a clinician examine you rather than wait.


- **A node that does not settle.** MedlinePlus advises contacting a clinician when nodes do not get smaller after several weeks or keep growing, feel hard, irregular or fixed in place, or come with fever, night sweats or unexplained weight loss \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003097.htm) \].
- **An unexplained node or enlarged spleen with B symptoms.** UK guidance from NICE says to consider a suspected cancer referral for adults with unexplained swollen nodes or an enlarged spleen, taking into account fever, night sweats, shortness of breath, itching or weight loss. For Hodgkin lymphoma it adds pain in a lymph node after drinking alcohol \[[17](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12/chapter/Recommendations-organised-by-site-of-cancer) \].
- **A persistent blood count change with a node or symptoms.** A high lymphocyte count, anemia or low platelets that stays abnormal on a repeat CBC, together with any of the signs above, is the kind of picture that leads to a lymph node exam, imaging and possibly a biopsy \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].
- **B symptoms with no swollen node.** The 2023 review says these alone should not trigger a targeted lymphoma workup. Instead, each symptom has its own standard workup, which would be expected to uncover lymphoma if it were the cause \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].


### Same-day red flags


Get emergency care for swelling of the face, neck, arms or upper chest with trouble breathing. Lymphoma in the chest can press on the large vein that drains the head and arms, which the American Cancer Society describes as life-threatening and needing treatment right away. Lymphoma in the chest can also cause coughing, trouble breathing or chest pain or pressure \[[15](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \]. The same pressure can cause a change in alertness. A lymphoma in the brain can cause headache, trouble thinking, weakness in part of the body or seizures, which also need urgent care \[[15](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \].


## How long can you have lymphoma without knowing?


It depends on the type. The National Cancer Institute divides non-Hodgkin lymphoma into indolent types, which grow and spread slowly and have few signs and symptoms, and aggressive types, which grow quickly and have signs and symptoms that can be severe \[[5](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lymphoma/patient/adult-nhl-treatment-pdq) \]. Slow-growing lymphomas can go unnoticed for a long time, and the American Cancer Society notes that non-Hodgkin lymphoma sometimes causes no symptoms until it grows quite large \[[15](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/non-hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/signs-symptoms.html) \]. People with aggressive lymphoma often describe rapidly enlarging nodes and marked B symptoms \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].


For a node you can feel, how long it has been there is one of the most useful facts you can bring to an appointment. A review in American Family Physician gives this guidance on timing \[[11](https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2016/1201/p896.html) \]:


- A swollen node present for less than two weeks, or for more than 12 months without changing in size, has a low likelihood of being cancer. Low-grade Hodgkin lymphoma and indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma are exceptions, though both usually come with other body-wide symptoms.
- When cancer seems unlikely after an exam, a localized swollen node can be watched for four weeks.
- Swelling for longer than four to six weeks, and a node that has not returned to normal after eight to 12 weeks, are among the listed risk factors for cancer. So are age over 40, swelling in two or more areas of the body, a node above the collarbone, and fever, night sweats, weight loss or an enlarged liver or spleen.


Nodes from an infection often take a while to shrink. MedlinePlus notes that a node may not return to its normal size for several weeks after the soreness goes away \[[16](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003097.htm) \]. A COVID-19 vaccine can cause reactive swelling of nodes in the armpit for up to 10 weeks afterward \[[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10042228/) \].


## Which tests to bring to a clinician


If you are worried, a clinician will start with a history and an exam of your lymph nodes, liver and spleen, then decide what tests to order. If a CBC is already done, bring the full report, including the differential, along with any earlier results for comparison. A change over time often says more than a single value.


When lymphoma is suspected or being worked up, the National Cancer Institute and American Cancer Society list these blood tests \[[5](https://www.cancer.gov/types/lymphoma/patient/adult-nhl-treatment-pdq) \]\[[6](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/hodgkin-lymphoma/detection-diagnosis-staging/how-diagnosed.html) \]:


Test What it adds


[CBC with differential and platelets](https://mitohealth.com/products/complete-blood-count-cbc-with-differential-and-platelet-count) Red cells, white cells by type, and platelets. Shows anemia, cytopenias or a high lymphocyte count


[Comprehensive metabolic panel](https://mitohealth.com/products/comprehensive-metabolic-panel-cmp) Kidney and liver function, and calcium


[LDH](https://mitohealth.com/products/lactate-dehydrogenase-ldh) A general marker of cell turnover and tissue damage, often checked once lymphoma is diagnosed


[ESR](https://mitohealth.com/products/erythrocyte-sedimentation-rate-esr) A general measure of inflammation, often checked when Hodgkin lymphoma is suspected


None of these tests can confirm lymphoma. The CBC is the useful starting point because it is the one most likely to show a change worth following, and it shows whether another cause, such as infection or iron deficiency, explains how you feel. If a CBC shows something that persists, or if a node or symptoms do not settle, the next steps are an exam, imaging and a biopsy, which a clinician orders.


Questions worth asking at the visit:


- Does this node need a biopsy now, or is it reasonable to recheck it in a few weeks?
- Is anything in my CBC abnormal, and should it be repeated?
- Could an infection, a recent vaccine or a medicine explain the swelling?
- If we wait, what change in size, feel or symptoms should bring me back sooner?

## Frequently asked questions


### Can a blood test detect lymphoma?


No routine blood test detects or rules out lymphoma. The American Cancer Society says blood tests are not used to diagnose it. A blood count, LDH or ESR can show changes that prompt a closer look, and the diagnosis is then made by a biopsy, most often of a lymph node.


### What does a CBC look like with lymphoma?


Often it looks normal. When it is abnormal, the changes can include anemia, a low platelet count, a low white cell count or a high lymphocyte count. None of these is specific to lymphoma. Infection, iron deficiency, medicines and many other conditions cause the same changes far more often.


### Can you have lymphoma with normal blood work?


Yes. A 2023 review of lymphoma workup in general practice notes that many people with lymphoma, even aggressive lymphoma, have a normal blood count, and that normal blood tests should not be used to rule lymphoma out. A lump or symptoms that do not go away still need a visit, whatever the blood work shows.


### How long can you have lymphoma without knowing?


It depends on the type. The National Cancer Institute describes indolent lymphomas as slow growing with few signs or symptoms, and aggressive lymphomas as fast growing with symptoms that can be severe. Slow-growing types can go unnoticed for a long time, while aggressive types usually cause symptoms or a growing lump within weeks to months.


### What blood tests are done if lymphoma is suspected?


A complete blood count, a blood chemistry panel covering kidney and liver function, and an LDH level are standard, and an ESR is often added for suspected Hodgkin lymphoma. Doctors may also test for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. These tests help plan care. They do not make the diagnosis.


### Is a high white blood cell count a sign of lymphoma?


It can be, but it is usually not. Infection, inflammation, allergic reactions, smoking, stress and some medicines raise the white count much more often. A count that stays high on repeat testing, especially with a high lymphocyte count, swollen nodes or night sweats, is worth taking to a clinician.
